content: An iron lung is a large mechanical device designed to assist individuals in breathing when their natural ability to do so is impaired, either due to loss of muscle control or when the effort required to breathe exceeds their physical capacity. The patient is placed inside the central chamber of the iron lung, which is a cylindrical steel drum. The head and neck remain outside the chamber through an opening that is sealed to maintain an airtight environment around the rest of the body. The iron lung is a non-invasive form of respiratory support. It was invented by Philip Drinker and Louis Agassiz Shaw at the Harvard School of Public Health, initially to treat coal gas poisoning. However, its most notable application occurred during the mid-20th century, particularly in the treatment of poliomyelitis (polio). Polio often caused paralysis, including of the diaphragm, the primary muscle responsible for breathing. Patients with diaphragmatic paralysis were unable to breathe independently and were placed in iron lungs to survive. The first recorded use of an iron lung occurred on October 12, 1928, at Boston Children’s Hospital, where it successfully revived a child suffering from respiratory failure within seconds of use. This event significantly increased the popularity of the device, which became known as the Drinker Respirator. In 1931, John Haven Jack Emerson introduced an improved version of the iron lung. His design was smaller, lighter, quieter, more reliable, and less expensive than the original Drinker model. However, this led to a legal dispute with Drinker and Harvard, who accused Emerson of patent infringement. During the legal proceedings, Emerson demonstrated that all aspects of Drinker's patents had been previously patented by others, leading to the invalidation of Drinker's patents. Emerson's version of the iron lung became widely adopted, and during the peak of polio outbreaks in the 1940s and 1950s, entire hospital wards were filled with rows of these devices. The widespread implementation of polio vaccination programs in the mid-20th century drastically reduced the incidence of the disease, leading to a sharp decline in the use of iron lungs. This method quickly gained popularity across Europe and eventually worldwide, as it proved to be more effective and less restrictive than the iron lung. Today, the iron lung occupies a marginal role in respiratory therapy. These devices are generally more effective and allow greater freedom of movement for patients and easier access for caregivers. Although the use of iron lungs has become rare, some patients continue to rely on these devices, often in home settings, despite challenges in sourcing replacement parts. A modern adaptation of the iron lung, known as Biphasic Cuirass Ventilation, has been developed.
